source.title: On Avoiding Local Minima Using Gradient Descent With Large Learning Rates
source.authors: Amirkeivan Mohtashami; Martin Jaggi; Sebastian U. Stich

record.file_problem: The text contains the full paper and appendices. There are minor apparent typos, but no material cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own comparisons of learning-rate conditions and argues that large learning rates affect optimization trajectories beyond their effect on stochastic noise. It does not measure the catalog’s train/test generalization-gap claim directly.
record.gate_note: The paper measures training and test accuracy in some experiments, but the reported outcomes test optimization and convergence-point behavior under learning-rate and noise conditions, not the claim versions’ named effects on the training/test gap or memorization. The cited generalization literature is prior work, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-rate effects on optimization, not any of V1–V8. Its accuracy comparisons vary learning rate and batch repetition, without comparing batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets. Its sharp-region escape results do not measure magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps. Related generalization findings appear as background.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that large learning rates affect optimization beyond amplifying stochastic noise. They prove escape and avoidance results for specified function classes and present neural-network evidence consistent with escaping sharp regions. They explicitly leave whether the avoided minima generalize better or worse outside their scope.
record.recipe_differences: Studies large-learning-rate effects on optimization trajectories and local-minimum avoidance, rather than memorization or generalization-gap interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate changes convergence and trajectory; repeating mini-batches to amplify stochastic noise improves results relative to standard low-rate SGD but does not close the performance gap with high-rate SGD. In the no-momentum, no-weight-decay experiment, repeats do not improve performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.1 and Appendix M report better training and test accuracy with learning rate 0.01 than 0.001 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Ten batch repeats at the smaller rate improve performance but do not close the difference, despite matching the longer small-rate run's update count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing stochasticity through batch repetition does not fully reproduce the performance benefit of a larger learning rate in these ResNet-18 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix N reports that the larger learning rate also performs better without momentum and weight decay, while batch repeats provide no improvement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of batch repetition depends on the training recipe, while the tested learning-rate advantage persists without momentum and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.2 and Figure 7 show that warm-started full-batch GD with a larger learning rate follows a different trajectory and initially increases training loss; subsequently reducing the rate does not restore the smaller-rate trajectory.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large learning rates can alter deterministic optimization trajectories and produce behavior consistent with escaping sharp regions.

record.problems: The generalization-gap versions are outside the paper’s scope. Neural-network evidence uses a single stated architecture, ResNet-18 without batch normalization, on CIFAR datasets; the trajectory experiment is deliberately warm-started near a minimum. Numerical accuracy values are presented in plots without textual values, and the described SGD results are averaged over 3 runs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the study’s measured training/test accuracy is used to compare optimization and learning-rate conditions, not to test any version’s named generalization-gap behavior. Figure-only accuracy curves do not supply claim-version results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Held-out error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipes that mitigate those effects.
Dropout effects on held-out error and their dependence on data size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Replace the record's tests/T5 classification with discusses/T6. No claim-linked rows or verdicts are warranted. The reason is the absence of the specific comparisons V1–V8 require, rather than a general requirement to measure a train/test gap.

versions.untested_parts: Memorizing random labels, natural-label test accuracy relative to chance, and coexistence of memorization and generalization.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error as a function of width.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and held-out performance under optimizer tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout intervention effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the train/test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
